input_types._why_this_exists: ADDED 2026-10-03. Until now the registry had a `fact_types` vocabulary and no `input_types` one, so `consumes.inputs[].type` was free text that nothing could check: R4 only compares a consumer's declared type against the producer's when the input carries a `from` edge, and 34 of 41 inputs do not. The two mistakes this made possible were measured, not guessed -- `net.pcap.analyse` and `net.pcap.selfparse` declared `capture: pcap`, and `mobile.apk.static` declared `apk: apk`, where `pcap` and `apk` are FACT types meaning an ALREADY-PARSED record set, while those three inputs are paths to files on disk. A file is a `path_ref`; what a reader makes of it is a fact.
input_types.path_ref: a filesystem path to an artefact the caller supplies. Never the artefact's contents -- that is what a fact is.
input_types.string: a text literal the caller supplies: a URL, a function name, a selector.
input_types.address: an address in the target's own address space, hex string, never reused across rebuilds.
input_types.token: a compact JOSE/JWT supplied as text. Never a live credential.
input_types.structure: a typed record the caller builds; the entry declares its fields.
input_types.structure[]: a batch of typed records. Needs envelope.batch (R9) because this class of API drops items silently.
input_types.lab_workdir: a directory the mission created for its own case. Not a caller-supplied file, which is why it is not a path_ref.
input_types.lab_target: a lab-chosen target the runner resolves from its own id list, not from anything the caller passes.

net_requirements.none: this capability runs with no network access at all; it is what 27 of 27 entries declare today
net_requirements.any: this capability cannot run without network access

lanes.debug: the debugging lane: a locally authored target under a named process, a loopback capture, or an isolated VM
lanes.bounty: the bounty lane: an in-scope third-party asset under the program rules

schema._two_net_fields: requires.net and reach.net are DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, and a mutation sweep flagged them as a contradiction when they are not. requires.net asks whether the capability NEEDS the network to run; reach.net declares whether it TOUCHES the network. net.pcap.analyse is the case that proves it: its probe runs tshark against a local capture and needs no network (requires.net none, correct), while its lab negative control is a CA-trust check, which is a network effect (reach.net true, and its own reach note says so). Reading one as the other is how a capability ends up escalating for the wrong reason.

question_types.Q1.identify: what is this file, is it packed, what is its shape
question_types.Q2.locate: where is the code that does X
question_types.Q3.behaviour: what does it actually do at runtime -- needs a device or a debugger
question_types.Q4.data: what is in this capture / image / dump
question_types.Q5.vuln-shape: where does it trust something it should not
question_types.Q7.origin: what changed between these two builds

baseline.note: The validator pins this count. A capability may only leave capabilities[] by appearing in retired[] with a reason, because deleting an island used to make the registry validate CLEANER rather than louder.
baseline.note_unused_fact_types: MEASURED 2026-10-02, and it corrects a natural misreading. A query for declared fact types produced by no capability returns four: apk, pcap, token, evidence_source. The first three look like dead declarations, and it is tempting to conclude the three matching capabilities (mobile.apk.static, net.pcap.analyse, crypto.jose.parse) do not declare what they produce. They DO -- all three declare their facts, and all three now carry an invoke. The types are unused because the capabilities declaring them have never RUN IN A MISSION, not because their output is unspecified. evidence_source is a different thing entirely: it is a capability attribute used to count independent instruments, not an artifact any capability emits, so it must never be counted here.
baseline.note_q5_unreachable:
MEASURED END TO END 2026-10-02, and it is a shape problem rather than a missing tool. Q5.vuln-shape has no reachable instrument. Its only target-scoped candidate, fuzz.differential.parse, declares two seed inputs whose producers are crypto.jose.parse and forensics.memory.artefact -- and both producers are observed and correctly wired. Verified on the real binaries rather than by reading: crypto.jose.parse invokes crypto-lab/tools/analyze.mjs --file {target} --json, and pointed at a PE it refuses with 'not a compact JWS: expected 3 dot-separated segments, got 2' and EXITS 3, which its own success_when already documents as bad input. Pointed at a real compact JWS it exits 0. forensics.memory.artefact invokes forensics-lab/tools/analyze.mjs --target {target}.

So neither producer is broken. They refuse correctly when handed the wrong KIND of thing, and that is the whole problem: mission.ps1 has one -Target, and this axis needs three different kinds of subject -- a JOSE token, a forensic memory image, and a lab target. Q5 is not dark because a tool is missing. It is dark because the mission can name exactly one artefact and Q5 needs three heterogeneous ones.

Two refutations are kept because both looked right first. First: 'these labs build their own fixtures, so no extra parameter is needed' is true of the LOOPS -- crypto-lab/tools/loop.mjs reads only --json and generates its own tokens, and forensics-lab/tools/loop.mjs:38 hardcodes const TARGET = path.join(WORK, 'target') -- but the invoke blocks point at the inner ANALYSERS, which do take an external subject. The loop and the instrument are different things and a mission calls the instrument. Second: 'fuzz.differential.parse wants two artefacts, so it needs a peer selector' is also true and also not the blocker, because its two missing inputs are not two paths; they are a token and a structure produced upstream.

What would light the axis is now stated precisely: a mission able to name MORE THAN ONE artefact with HETEROGENEOUS types. A second path would not help -- native.function.match is the only capability that wants two of the same thing and it is not on this axis. Naming the shape exactly is what separates this from the speculative -Artefact parameter considered and correctly rejected earlier, when the premise had not been measured.

The misattribution risk was checked and does not exist: a PE substituted into the JOSE analyser exits 3, so a mission records a loud failure rather than crediting the lab's own token to the mission's target.
baseline.note_q5_three_reasons:
Q5.vuln-shape is dark for THREE INDEPENDENT REASONS, and the third is the one that matters. (1) Its only target-scoped candidate, fuzz.differential.parse, declares its subject a lab_target. (2) Its two seed producers are lab analysers whose subjects are lab-built scenario directories, verified by measurement rather than by reading. (3) THAT CANDIDATE DECLARES ITSELF NOT COVERABLE BY A GRANT -- gate.requires_verdict is false, and gate.Get-GrantableIds grants only where it is true. Measured: crypto.jose.parse hit exactly this wall, refused as skipped_not_in_grant with a correct invoke and a correctly seeded fact.

Reason (3) is not an engineering problem and must not be solved as one. Flipping the flag would be weakening a safety marker to improve a metric, which is the error this project has refused all session. It is recorded as an OWNER DECISION on the three capabilities carrying it -- crypto.jose.parse, re.corpus.solve and fuzz.differential.parse -- and none of them had a reason recorded until now, which is itself the defect R22 closes: a capability can declare itself unrunnable by a grant without saying why.

evidence_families._definition: Which FAMILY of instrument produced a fact. Independence is a property of the INSTRUMENT, not of the tool id and not of this label: two capabilities that drive the same instrument are ONE opinion however they are labelled, and two different decompilers are also one opinion (fact_types.evidence_source says exactly this). The enumerated values below are the permitted set; R18 fails the run on anything else, and R18 also fails when two capabilities sharing one instrument declare different families. Correcting a label here cannot change what the mission gate believes about independence -- the gate must derive the family axis from the instrument -- but a registry that disagrees with itself is a registry nobody can reason about.
evidence_families.decompiler: reconstructs executable code into a higher-level language: Hex-Rays IDA and Ghidra both land here, and two of them agreeing is ONE opinion held twice, not corroboration
evidence_families.static-analysis: NOT a separate family. Retained only so the value is not silently re-used; no capability should carry it, because on this estate it existed solely to relabel one idalib-mcp capability and thereby manufacture a second family
evidence_families.dynamic-observation: watches a running subject: a live page over CDP, a live process
evidence_families.dynamic-instrumentation: injects into or attaches to a live process to observe or alter it
evidence_families.structural-parser: decodes a self-describing container without executing it: JOSE/JWT, zip, png
evidence_families.capture-analysis: reads recorded traffic rather than live traffic
evidence_families.artefact-parser: reads host artefacts left on disk: prefetch, SRUM, registry hives
evidence_families.package-inspection: reads a packaged artefact as built: APK manifest, DEX, resources
evidence_families.binary-similarity: matches functions across two binaries by scoring, without proving equivalence
evidence_families.differential-oracle: compares two implementations of the same parser and treats a disagreement as the finding
evidence_families.practice: solving self-built exercises; proves technique, not transfer
evidence_families.disassembler: reconstructs a machine instruction stream WITHOUT lifting it to a high-level language: capstone and similar code-generation libraries. Distinct from 'decompiler' because it performs no lifting, no type recovery and no control-flow reconstruction -- it is the only family here that states an OPERAND WIDTH, which is measured, not assumed: see native.disasm.capstone's negative control and the pairing study. Added 2026-10-02 after measuring that capstone independently identified the exact addresses Ghidra left as unresolved DAT_ references AND carried the byte-vs-dword width that Ghidra's output omitted. THIS IS NOT THE static-analysis RELABEL ESCAPE: that escape re-declared ONE instrument under a second name, which R18 also blocks by instrument identity. capstone is a genuinely different library with no decompiler in its lineage. What it does NOT buy is confirmation of MEANING -- it corroborates structure and operands, not what the code does.
evidence_families.certificate-verifier: A certificate-verifier decides whether a byte range is a valid encoding of a CERTIFICATE. It is not structural-parser: that family parses a PE IMAGE structure, while this decides whether the bytes inside the SECURITY directory are DER at all, using a different implementation (OpenSSL) from the one that located them (pefile). And it is not trust: no member of this family checks that a chain roots anywhere or that a digest matches a file. der_parsed:true means well-formed ASN.1, which is a far weaker statement than signed.
evidence_families.packet-reader: A packet-reader parses the capture FILE FORMAT itself -- global header, per-packet headers, then enough of the link and network layers to count. It is not capture-analysis, which means shelling out to a dissector, and not structural-parser, which means reading an executable image. Two readers agreeing on a capture is agreement between two implementations of the format, which is the only kind of agreement that is worth calling corroboration.
evidence_families.format-reader: A format-reader parses a container's structure using a SEPARATE IMPLEMENTATION from the one other readers use, so agreement between them is corroboration rather than a restatement. rabin2 is a C tool with its own PE format layer; pefile is a Python library. This family is named for the implementation being independent, not for the file type, because the file type is not what the independence gate is counting.

_comment: Capability contracts, so an orchestrator can compose labs it can introspect. This is NOT an inventory -- manifests/tools.json records what is installed. A capability here states what it consumes, the typed facts it produces, what it requires, what it proves, what it does NOT prove, and a negative control that must fail. 'state: observed' means the probe below was actually run; the summary is what it printed. Verify with: python scripts/registry-verify.py. Orchestrate with: powershell -File scripts\mission.ps1 -Action Run ...

fact_types.address: an address in the target's own address space, hex string, never reused across rebuilds
fact_types.string: a text literal recovered from the target
fact_types.structure: a typed record: named fields, each with an offset and a type
fact_types.bytes_ref: a pointer to content-addressed bytes under E:\missions\ or a lab out dir; the bytes are not inlined
fact_types.verdict: an outcome class from a closed enumeration: confirmed | likely | speculative | unresolved | refused
fact_types.path_ref: a filesystem path to an artifact; never the artifact's contents
fact_types.apk: a parsed Android package manifest or dex summary
fact_types.token: a parsed JOSE/JWT: header, claims, signature presence -- never a live credential
fact_types.evidence_source: which FAMILY of instrument produced a fact. Independence is about the family, not the tool id: ghidra.decompile and ida.decompile are both 'decompiler' and therefore cannot corroborate each other.
fact_types.rva: a relative virtual address: an offset from the image base, NOT an address. It becomes an address only when added to a measured runtime module base, and an RVA handed over unrebased faults rather than misbehaving quietly. Added 2026-10-03 because native.pe.container own note said an RVA is not an address while the field was declared `address` -- a fact typed as something it is not is worse than an untyped one, because every consumer of `address` assumes it can be dereferenced.
fact_types.boolean: true or false, and nothing else. Added 2026-10-03: four facts declared `structure` or `verdict` were emitting bare booleans (measured: identical_inputs false, signed false, packed false), and `verdict` is a five-value outcome enumeration, so a boolean wearing it was a lie a reader could not detect.
fact_types.number: a scalar measurement: a score, a ratio, a count. NOT a finding and NOT an outcome class. Added 2026-10-03 after measuring rules_matched 14 declared `verdict` -- the entry own note had already said a COUNT IS NOT A FINDING, and the type said otherwise.
fact_types.structure[]: an ORDERED LIST of records, as distinct from `structure`, which is one record. Added 2026-10-03: five facts bound to list-valued stdout keys (matches, pairs, insns, rip_operands, sections) were declared `structure`, so a consumer asking for a named field would find nothing where a list was. One character of vocabulary separated a record from a list of records, and nothing refused the difference.

inputs.note: The other edge is real too and is kept: decompile.mjs accepts a function-name-OR-address (native-lab/tools/decompile.mjs:4,15,31-39) and resolves a name to an address itself. Declared separately so the two typed facts are not conflated.

unbound.reason: P8 measured this rather than binding it: native-lab/tools/decompile.mjs writes NO file. Its whole output is stdout JSON {ok, addr, code, refs}; there is no fs.write in it at all. The *.c export belongs to the Ghidra path instead -- scripts/ghidra/ExportDecompile.java:67 writes safeName(name)+'.c' per function, and that artifact (native.ghidra.c) IS now bound to a fact_map. So this entry is kept as the declared name but marked unbound with the reason, rather than bound to something that does not exist.

tools.name: idalib-mcp
tools.verify_note: NOT EXECUTED BY check-requires-tools.py, and says so. This is an MCP device or a browser surface, not a command line: there is no shell invocation that would prove it present, and inventing one would produce a probe that passes without testing anything. Declared unverifiable rather than given a probe that cannot fail.

reach.note: decompile itself only reads. The PROCESS it runs in does not: idalib-mcp can write a 2.7 MB .i64 to an arbitrary path via idb_save, which its own --unsafe tagging does NOT cover. So the trust boundary is the server, not the tool.

gate_must_not_delegate: server flag --unsafe
server flag --profile
http:POST /config
capabilities.gate_must_not_delegate_why: Measured on this host, not read: on a worker started WITHOUT --unsafe (py_eval absent from tools/list), one unauthenticated loopback form POST -- POST /config with apply_profile=1&profile_text=py_eval -- made py_eval callable and it returned 2. http.py:93 snapshots ORIGINAL_TOOLS at import time, BEFORE idalib_server.py:285-289 deletes the unsafe tools, and http.py:442-446 rebuilds tools.methods from that stale snapshot; _check_api_request (mcp.py:303-328) accepts any request carrying no Origin header, so no token is needed. The result is persisted into the IDB netnode $ ida_mcp.enabled_tools (http.py:447), so the policy travels inside the sample's .i64. Two further holes: idb_open/idb_list are `protected` from --profile (idalib_server.py:57-60), and the supervisor never applies --profile to its own registry (idalib_supervisor.py:1498-1499 only forwards it to workers), so a 'read-only' profile still grants arbitrary-path file access. Our gate enforces this; the server's own flags do not.

covers: server flag --unsafe
server flag --profile
http:POST /config

select.note: Takes the first recovered non-sub_ name. The first candidate is a hypothesis, not a conclusion: the verdict gates still require a second capability before anything is called confirmed.

proves: that a named function's machine code decompiles to the C shown, on those exact bytes

evidence_binding.reason: Honest state, and now with the blocker NAMED rather than described. Re-measured 2026-10-03: `python scripts/assert-probes.py native.ida.decompile native.ida.list_functions --save-evidence ...` reports `SKIP  <id>: driven through the idalib-mcp MCP device, not a CLI command` -- so the runner never executes these two probes and there is nothing to hash. The instrument is reachable (the lab loop `node native-lab/tools/loop.mjs --only=decompile` runs it), but a loop a human starts by hand is not a probe the harness can re-run, and pretending otherwise is what R17 exists to refuse. Three ways out, none taken unilaterally: (a) an idalib CLI entry point that writes a JSON artifact, (b) a save-evidence path through the MCP device, or (c) demote the entry. Until one exists this entry's 'observed' rests on last_summary and the lab README in provenance.record. R17 accepts exactly this marker and no softer one, so the day a hash exists this must be replaced, not left.

probe.distinct_probe_note: SCOPED, and this replaced an IDENTICAL probe.command shared with the other IDA capability. Measured before: native.ida.decompile and native.ida.list_functions both pointed at `node native-lab/tools/loop.mjs`, which genuinely exercises both -- so neither was a false probe, but a break in `decompile` reddened BOTH entries and neither could be blamed. loop.mjs now takes --only=<tool>; verified both directions: --only=decompile runs the decompile assertions, --only=list_funcs runs ZERO of them while still proving its own two. The default with no flag still covers both, and remains the integration check. A shared probe is legal; a probe that cannot LOCALISE a fault is not much of a probe.
probe.produces_note: Added 2026-10-04. Before this the entry declared no artifact, so assert-proces matched STRINGS ONLY and said so on every OK: 'NOT a claim that the instrument ran: a stub which prints them satisfies it.' The loop now writes this file on every exit path, so the verdict checks the FILESYSTEM. PER-TOOL path on purpose -- both entries run the same loop with a different --only flag, and one shared path would let one tool's run satisfy the other's declaration.

negative_control.why: must yield code:null plus an error field, never code. Asserted by native-lab/tools/loop.mjs.
negative_control.plan_note: DECLARED A PLAN, NOT A CONTROL, ON 2026-10-02. Rule R21 refuses prose in negative_control.command, because a control nobody can execute cannot fail and therefore passes forever. The sentence is kept here rather than deleted: it is the negative design, which is real knowledge, and this project has been burned often enough by deleting things to keep. What this entry no longer claims is that it has a working control. It does not.
negative_control.measured: measured 2026-10-02. exit 1, {ok:false, addr:'0xDEADBEEF', error:'Decompilation failed at 0xdeadbeef'} with NO code field, against exit 0 and 400+ chars of recovered C on the same tool for a real function. The control discriminates, so it can fail.
negative_control.expect_output_note: THIS REFUTES THE PLAN REASON IT REPLACES, which read 'There is no CLI that takes an address'. decompile.mjs line 33 takes '<function-name-or-address>' and line 41 branches on /^0x/i. The registry had the tool's own usage string in the repo and recorded the opposite of it.

Two typed facts, not one nested one.

Labelling both idalib-mcp capabilities 'decompiler' makes the structured field agree with the prose. This label is documentation for a human reader: the mission gate must derive the family axis from the instrument, not from this string.

negative_control.measured: MEASURED 2026-10-04, mutation-tested rather than merely run, and the polarity was corrected by rule R5 rather than by opinion. R5 requires a negative control to declare a NON-ZERO expect_exit, because a control that must exit 0 proves nothing: an instrument that had stopped enforcing would also exit 0 and the harness would read that as a pass. Live: the gate returns HTTP 401 {"error":"bad-signature"} and the control exits 2. Mutant: short-circuiting `if (!timingSafeEqHex(sig, signBody(body, ts)))` in web-reverse/lab/server.mjs makes the SAME control exit 0, with the message 'the gate ACCEPTED a request signed with the wrong key'. So the control is discriminating in both directions -- it reports the refusal as a failure and reports the acceptance as a pass, which is what makes its non-zero expected exit meaningful. The first version of the script had the polarity the intuitive way round and registry-verify.py caught it within seconds of the declaration.

negative_control.measured:
measured 2026-10-02: exit 4 with 'unexpected: MISSING_EXP, MISSING_AUD, MISSING_JTI, NO_KID, MISSING_NBF'. Widening --expect to all six ids exits 0 on the SAME token, so one token is a pass under one expectation and a failure under another -- which is the property: a verifier that stops checking everything must fail loudly.

The control is two steps, so it is a FILE. Written inline as `node -e 'import(...)'` it came back mangled -- PowerShell re-quotes native-command arguments, the import specifier was altered, and the analyser reported 'expected 3 dot-separated segments, got 1'. A probe that no longer reaches the tool it exists to guard is the worst possible outcome for a control, and the fix is the same one native.pe.authenticode needed: a file, not a shell string.

sibling_control.expect_output: the corroboration rule is LIVE and it was shown refusing
sibling_control.why: an independent source GROUP is removed from a two-group claim and the verdict must degrade from confirmed to possible. Independence here is a group from triage.mjs's SOURCE_GROUPS = {MEM, AM, PF, SRUM}, NOT a file, timestamp, host, offset or hash. capabilities.scope_note: SCANS TEXT THIS REPOSITORY AUTHORED, PLUS THE SYNTHETIC NEGATIVE CONTROL. It reads .md and .py files under a path the caller names and emits JSON/Markdown findings. capabilities.composition_note: WHY IT IS A CAPABILITY AND NOT A NICE-TO-HAVE. wiki/methods/skill-adoption-checklist.md was hand-written today with ten blocks, of which three are greps a human must remember to run. ANYTHING ABOUT A TARGET BINARY. It reads instruction text, not code semantics. capa and FLOSS answer that question and this does not.

THAT THE INSTALL IS REPRODUCIBLE OFFLINE. `uv tool install git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git` reaches the network and pulls typer, yara-python, tiktoken, truststore and zstandard. An air-gapped station gets nothing from this entry.

THAT A HIGH SCORE MEANS THE SCANNED CONTENT IS HOSTILE. MEASURED FALSE POSITIVE, and it is the most important limitation of this entry. Pointing it at mcp/debugger-router returns score 100, severity CRITICAL, recommendation DO_NOT_INSTALL -- and that directory is OUR OWN server. The cause is mechanical: it holds 3,604 files, of which 3,601 are inside .venv and 1,536 are __pycache__ bytecode, and the scan returned 4,916 findings, EVERY ONE of them attributed to file=None line 1. A finding with no file is not evidence about any file. Narrower tests locate the trigger precisely: a 2-file directory gives 0 issues, forty ordinary python modules give 0, a synthetic skill directory with 30 dependency files beside its SKILL.md gives 0, and this arsenal's own skills/ gives 0 at 100 percent coverage. So the scanner is sound on skill-shaped content and degenerates on a vendored dependency tree, where it cannot attribute what it found and scores the whole directory CRITICAL anyway. **An operator who ran this over a repository and reported the number would have reported our own router as hostile, and every specific finding they could have acted on was unattributed.** The correct use is a skill directory, never a dependency tree, and a CRITICAL verdict with file=None findings is a malfunction to investigate rather than a result to act on.
capabilities.analysis_note: THE CONTROL FAILURE WORTH REMEMBERING, and it arrived from OUTSIDE this harness. That is the third category the charter names -- a correct control quoted as if it were an end-to-end result -- and it is reassuring that a third-party tool committed it too. The fix is not to distrust the score but to make the incompatibility LOUD, and the tool already can: ---fail-on-incomplete returned exit 2 on exactly that run and 0 with ---no-llm. So the probe now carries both gate flags, and analysis_completeness is a produced fact rather than a log line nobody reads.

capabilities.title: Intercept a self-built Windows PE at its entry point with Frida 17.17.0, by loading the script BEFORE resuming the main thread
capabilities.scope_note: SELF-BUILT TARGETS ONLY, and the reason this is a separate entry from dynamic.win.frida is exactly the honesty that entry records. dynamic.win.frida drives the `frida` CLI, which spawn-gates and resolves exports but does NOT intercept: on Windows the CLI resumes the main thread BEFORE the injected script loads, so the target runs to completion first. This entry drives the Python API in the order spawn -> attach -> create_script -> load -> resume, and it DOES intercept. One instrument, two orderings, two claims -- and the difference is measured, not argued.
capabilities.composition_note: WHY A SIBLING RATHER THAN AN EDIT. Editing dynamic.win.frida to claim interception would make the entry describe something its registered probe does not do. The charter's rule is that a capability states what its probe proves; a capability whose probe cannot show the claim is a claim wearing a capability's clothes. So the CLI entry keeps its narrower, true does_not_prove and this entry carries the wider, also-true claim. native-lab/tools/frida_spawn_gate.py holds the recipe and is committed, because a recipe that lives only in %TEMP% is not a capability, it is a rumour.

capabilities.evidence_source_note: The SAME family as native.crosscompare.ghidra and nothing else. Deliberately a different family from every decompiler: it compares two implementations by content address rather than reconstructing either. That is what makes it the arsenal's only genuinely-different-family instrument on the native axis -- but it is honest about the limit, because it answers Q7.origin (what changed between two builds) and NOT Q2.locate (where is the code in this one). Registering it does not move the acceptance mission off unresolved, and the note exists to stop that being claimed.
capabilities.root_reason: Genuine root, and structurally so: it is handed two paths and compares them. Nothing else in this registry produces a SECOND build of a program -- the labs build binaries, but building is not comparing, and a mission that has run one builder still has no second artefact to diff against. It therefore consumes an input no upstream capability emits, which is exactly why it declares no typed edge and why the omission is a decision rather than an oversight.

not_callable.reason: NOT CALLABLE, AND THE REGISTRY REFUSED TO LET ME PRETEND OTHERWISE. I declared an invoke whose second binary came from a fact `pe.binary_pair` that nothing produces, expecting the round to skip loudly in the open. Two rules refused it and both were right. R10: an invoke whose consumes_fact is produced by no capability is a chain that can never fire, and a permanently dead invoke is worse than none -- it looks like a wired capability. R16 caught a second real bug in the same breath: I wrote the placeholder {input.peer} when the declared input is `dest`, so that literal string would have reached the command line verbatim. **The registry will not encode a capability that cannot run, which is the correct policy and cost me the shortcut.** The honest gap it exposes is architectural: Q7.origin asks what changed between TWO builds, and mission.ps1 has exactly ONE -Target. Nothing in this registry carries a second binary, so no two-artifact capability can be made callable until a peer-selector exists to produce one.
not_callable.measured_subject_matter: The subject EXISTS and was measured, which is why this is a plumbing gap rather than a missing corpus. crackme-corpus/out/c01-stringobf.exe and c01_stringobf.exe are two builds of one program differing in exactly FOUR bytes: TimeDateStamp 0x6abc5d71 = 2026-09-30 00:53:05 UTC against 0x6abc5bc8 = 2026-09-30 00:46:00 UTC, seven minutes apart, plus the same two bytes repeated at 0x1e2f4 in the checksum. `match-functions.ps1` on that pair returns matched 511 of 511, rate 100 percent, 0 renamed, identical_inputs FALSE -- which is exactly right: the code is identical and the files are not. This is the sharpest available illustration of the entry's own caveat that a content hash is not a similarity score and a match is not file-identity.
not_callable.what_would_close_it: A capability that takes a target and emits the corpus binary sharing its function-content signature -- a peer selector. It would publish `pe.binary_pair`, which is what this entry's invoke needs. Not built. Building it to make one entry callable, rather than because several questions need it, would be inventing scope; the honest next step is to find out whether Q7.origin is asked often enough to justify a two-artifact mission shape.

capabilities.title: Disassemble a self-built PE at an RVA and resolve RIP-relative operands WITH their widths, using no decompiler at all
capabilities.scope_note: SELF-AUTHORED TARGETS. It reads a PE with pefile, maps an RVA through the section table, and decodes bytes with capstone. It does not execute the target and does not lift instructions to a language. A non-executable section is REFUSED unless --force is passed.
capabilities.composition_note: WHY IT EXISTS, in one measurement. On crackme-corpus/out/c01-stringobf.exe main at RVA 0x1080: IDA Pro inlined the XOR key constants as 18/11/90 and 26/5/51; Ghidra left two of them as DAT_140017344 and DAT_140017342 with NO width, which is dangerous because read as the natural u32, DAT_140017342 is 734042; capstone, containing no decompiler whatsoever, emits `movzx r9d, byte ptr [rip+0x16259]` -> 0x140017342 byte=90 and `mov r8d, dword ptr [rip+0x16254]` -> 0x140017344 dword=11. Same values IDA propagated, plus the WIDTH, because the movzx prefix says byte and the bare mov says dword. **So it is not merely a second opinion on structure: it is the only one of the three instruments that states the fact whose absence made Ghidra's output a trap rather than merely incomplete.**

inputs.name: binary
inputs.note: a Windows PE. Measured: crackme-corpus/out/c01-stringobf.exe.

inputs.name: function
inputs.note: consumed as the RVA SOURCE only. The image-space address is NOT usable here and must be rebased: this tool takes --rva, never an address, because passing an address to a file-offset mapping is the mistake documented in does_not_prove.

facts.note: the decoded instruction stream as {addr, mnemonic, op_str} triples. Measured 40 instructions from RVA 0x1080, including `cmp dword ptr [rsp + 0xa0], 2` at 0x1400010a2 -- the argc==2 guard the decompilers both report as `if (argc == 2)`. RE-TYPED 2026-10-03 from `bytes_ref`. Measured: the 40 disassembled instructions are INLINED in stdout and the probe writes no file. `bytes_ref` is a pointer to content-addressed bytes whose bytes are not inlined, so this fact pointed at bytes that are not there.

every RIP-relative memory operand resolved to an absolute address WITH ITS WIDTH: {at, text, target, width, byte, dword}. This is the unique contribution. Measured: 0x140017342 width=byte value 90; 0x140017344 width=dword value 11; 0x140017343 width=byte value 51; 0x140017364 width=dword value 5. RE-TYPED 2026-10-03 from `structure`. Measured: rip_operands is a list of nine objects.
the containing section and whether IMAGE_SCN_MEM_EXECUTE (0x20000000) is set. Measured .text 0x60000020 executable, .rdata 0x40000040 not.

requires.install_note: Already installed in the system Python 3.14.7. No install, no disk cost. pefile 2024.8.26 is the same interpreter.

reach.proc_spawn_note: Declared because the probe and both controls invoke `python native-lab/tools/disasm.py` as a child process, which is the station's own interpreter reading a file. Nothing else spawns and no target executes -- exec_target stays false and that is the distinction the validator exists to keep honest.

proves: THAT A NON-DECOMPILER INSTRUMENT INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATES THE STRUCTURE of a locate claim. Measured with no decompiler in the lineage: `cmp dword ptr [rsp+0xa0], 2` at 0x1400010a2, and two calls to 0x140001000 with edx=0x12 and edx=0x1a -- matching the decompiled `argc == 2` guard and the decode-call lengths 18 and 26 that BOTH decompilers report.

THAT IT RESOLVES WHAT A DECOMPILER LEAVES BEHIND, INCLUDING THE WIDTH. The four RIP-relative operands it reports point at exactly the addresses Ghidra emitted as unresolved DAT_ references (0x140017342, 0x140017344, 0x140017343, 0x140017364) and it states that 0x140017342 is a BYTE load and 0x140017344 a DWORD load. Ghidra stated neither address's value nor its width; IDA stated the value but only by propagating a constant and discarding the width evidence.

THAT IT REFUSES NON-CODE. Measured: --rva 0x17000 lands in .rdata (Characteristics 0x40000040, no IMAGE_SCN_MEM_EXECUTE) and returns exit 2 with the section name and its characteristics, where the first version of this tool returned ok:true with 8 instructions decoded out of ASCII string bytes.
does_not_prove: WHAT THE CODE MEANS. These are instructions, not recovered logic: no lifting, no types, no control-flow reconstruction. It corroborates that a comparison and two calls exist at these addresses; it cannot say the program checks a password.

THAT THE ACCEPTANCE MISSION NOW CONFIRMS, and this is the honest limit. evidence_source is 'disassembler', a genuinely different family from 'decompiler', so a chain of IDA plus capstone would satisfy the gate's two-instrument two-family requirement. **Whether that is CORRECT depends on the claim, and the gate cannot currently tell claims apart.** For 'main compares argc to 2 and calls a decode routine twice', capstone genuinely corroborates and confirmation would be honest. For 'the XOR key is 11, 90, 5, 51', it also happens to corroborate here -- but only because constant propagation happens to be visible in the operand, and that is a property of this binary, not a general guarantee. Registering this family must not be read as having resolved the acceptance question, and the mission's unresolved verdict stands until someone runs the chain and reads whether the RESULT is defensible, not merely whether the gate turned green.

THAT AN RVA IS AN ADDRESS. --rva takes a relative virtual address and maps it through the section table. Passing an image-space address, or using an RVA as a raw file offset, yields zero instructions or garbage; the first draft of this script did exactly that and the wrapper now refuses rather than reporting an empty success.
ANYTHING ABOUT A THIRD-PARTY BINARY. Corpus targets only.

THAT ADDING THIS FAMILY RESOLVED THE ACCEPTANCE MISSION. MEASURED, AND IT DID NOT. The Q2.locate acceptance mission was re-run AFTER this entry and the `disassembler` family existed in the schema, and it still returned tier=unresolved with independence FAIL: '2 capabilities resolve to 1 instrument(s) [idalib-mcp] carrying 1 distinct family/families [decompiler]'. The planner never routed this entry, because it has no `invoke` block -- the same condition that leaves native.function.match, native.pe.packer and native.crosscompare.ghidra probeable but uncallable. **So four capabilities in this registry, including the only instrument in a genuinely different family, cannot be planned into a mission.** That is the correct outcome -- registering a family must not be able to turn a gate green on its own -- and it is also the next structural hole. Wiring this one would require the typed edge to carry an RVA, because this tool takes --rva and IDA's native.func.addr is an image-space address, so the conversion has to happen somewhere and putting it in the argv would be the joined-command-line pattern R10 exists to refuse.

THAT A NAME LOOKUP IS ALWAYS UNAMBIGUOUS. THE POSITIONAL WEAKNESS IS CLOSED; THIS IS WHAT REPLACES IT. select.by_name='main' fails LOUDLY instead of guessing: measured, planting a name that does not exist makes round 4 SKIP with the missing name printed, independence drop back to '2 capabilities resolve to 1 instrument(s) [idalib-mcp] carrying 1 family', and the verdict return unresolved with a non-zero exit. So the confirmed result genuinely depends on capstone finding `main`; it cannot silently pick whatever sits at a position. Verified unambiguous on this binary: 362 functions, exactly one named `main` at 0x140001080, and NO duplicate names at all. THE RESIDUAL, stated rather than hidden: a binary with two overloads both named `main` would resolve to the first, and there is no disambiguation key. The `main` string is also a REGISTRY-SIDE HYPOTHESIS about which function the claim is about -- it is checked against the analyser's own recovered name, which is the strongest available check without a semantic claim-to-function binding, and that binding is not built.

capabilities.title: Report whether a Windows PE carries an Authenticode certificate table, and decode its WIN_CERTIFICATE header -- without verifying anything
capabilities.scope_note: READ-ONLY on the target. Reads IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY from the PE optional header and, if present, the WIN_CERTIFICATE header it points at. It never executes a target and never contacts a network: no revocation checking, no chain building, no OCSP, no CRL.
capabilities.composition_note: WHY IT IS THE CHEAPEST REAL EXPANSION OF THE THINNEST AXIS. Coverage measured 2026-10-02 across the seven question types showed Q6 -- 'what token/signature/key handling is this' -- resting on ONE instrument, crypto.jose.parse, which is JOSE/JWT only. For a Windows PE the signature handling lives in the same optional header native.pe.packer and native.pe.container already read, so this costs no new dependency, no install and no disk. The trap it encodes is the one that makes this non-obvious: IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY's VirtualAddress is a FILE OFFSET, not an RVA, unlike every other data directory. Mapping it through the section table produces a plausible address in the wrong place.

reach.proc_spawn_note: Declared because the probe and both controls invoke `python headless-lab/tools/authenticode.py` as a child process. Nothing else spawns, exec_target stays false, and no network is touched -- which is the property that matters here, since real revocation checking would need one.

proves: THAT A CERTIFICATE TABLE IS PRESENT OR ABSENT, on a self-authored fixture and on a real binary. Measured: the fixture returns signed:true with security_offset 143872, dwLength 48, wRevision 0x200, wCertificateType 0x2, and its blob reading back the authored ASCII marker; every corpus binary returns signed:false with an empty directory. Two inputs, opposite answers, from the same code -- which is the only thing that makes 'unsigned' mean anything.

THAT THE WIN_CERTIFICATE HEADER DECODES, and that the FILE-OFFSET semantics of IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY are handled as such rather than as an RVA. That distinction is the whole reason this is an entry rather than four lines in triage.md.
does_not_prove: THAT THE BINARY IS TRUSTED, OR THAT ITS SIGNATURE IS VALID. NOTHING IS VERIFIED. No chain is built, no certificate is parsed, no hash is recomputed over the image, no revocation is checked, no timestamp is examined. `signed: true` means exactly 'there is a WIN_CERTIFICATE here'. A binary whose image was modified after signing still reads signed:true here, and the self-authored fixture reads signed:true with no key and no signature at all. Any trust decision needs a tool that actually verifies, and this is not one.
THAT AN ABSENCE MEANS UNSIGNED BY CHOICE. A repacked or tampered binary can have its certificate table stripped, which reads identically to one that was never signed. Absence is not provenance.
THAT THE PKCS#7 BLOB IS WELL FORMED. It is located and hashed, not parsed. The blob_sha256_prefix is an identity, not a validation.
ANYTHING ABOUT A THIRD-PARTY BINARY. Corpus targets only.

capabilities.composition_note:
REGISTERED BECAUSE AN AUDIT FOUND IT MISSING ENTIRELY. capa is installed and works headlessly, and searching the registry for the string 'capa' returned all 23 entries -- because the word appears inside 'capabilit*y*'. It had no entry at all. What makes it worth registering is the property this registry has been short of: it is TARGET-SCOPED. It takes a path, so a mission can actually route it, unlike the five capabilities whose subject is a token, a pcap, an APK, a loopback URL or a lab artefact.

Measured on c01-stringobf.exe, its 14 hits are 'change memory protection', 'PEB access', 'create or open file' -- those are BEHAVIOURS present in the code, not trust boundaries. capabilities.title: Independently parse a PE certificate table's bytes with OpenSSL ASN.1 and say whether they are DER
capabilities.scope_note: SELF-BUILT CORPUS AND FIXTURE TARGETS ONLY. It reads the file and shells out to openssl asn1parse on an extracted temporary .der, which is deleted in a finally block. No network, no execution of the target.
capabilities.composition_note:
ADDED BECAUSE INDEPENDENCE, NOT BECAUSE COVERAGE. Q6.crypto measured 1 of 2 callable capabilities working, and its single working instrument was native.pe.authenticode carrying family structural-parser -- one instrument, one family, so the independence gate could never pass there. This is a SECOND FAMILY answering a different question, not a second label on the first.

AND IT FOUND A REAL DISAGREEMENT, which is the strongest evidence in the registry for keeping it. native.pe.authenticode's own does_not_prove says it verifies nothing. Pointed at this repository's own signed fixture it reports dwLength=48, wRevision=0x200, revision_is_2_0=true -- a plausible, cheerful header. MEASURED, the 40-byte body is the ASCII string ARSENAL-FIXTURE-NOT-A-REAL-SIGNATURE and `openssl asn1parse -inform DER` rejects it outright: 'error:0680009B:asn1 encoding routines:ASN1_get_object:too long', exit 1.

Neither instrument is wrong. pefile is right about the header; OpenSSL is right about the DER. Only together do they say the thing that matters: the arsenal's own 'signed' fixture is not a signature, and an instrument reading only the header would never have noticed. That is what a second opinion is FOR, and it is not visible from either side alone.

inputs.name: binary
inputs.note: a Windows PE. The SECURITY directory stores a FILE OFFSET, not an RVA; this tool resolves it the same way native.pe.authenticode does and says so in its source rather than quietly agreeing with it.

facts.note: dwLength, wRevision, wCertificateType, revision_is_2_0, is_pkcs_signed_data, body_bytes. Measured on the fixture: dwLength 48, wRevision 0x200, wCertificateType 0x2, 40 body bytes.

TRI-STATE, and the three states are not interchangeable. true = OpenSSL parsed the bytes as DER. false = OpenSSL rejected them and reason says why. null = there is no SECURITY directory, so there is nothing to verify. 'nothing to verify' and 'what is there is not valid' are different findings and MUST NOT share a value -- collapsing them is how an unsigned binary gets reported as a broken signature. Measured: null on c01-stringobf.exe, false on the fixture, with reason 'ASN1_get_object:too long'.

requires.install_note: Both already present. Measured OpenSSL 3.5.7. No download, no build, no PATH change. Runs in well under a second against a fixture -- the cheapest capability in the arsenal, which is worth knowing because it makes this the natural second instrument to run whenever a first one reports something surprising.

reach.proc_spawn_note: Declared because it invokes openssl.exe as a child. fs_write is also true and honestly so: it writes a temporary .der under the system temp directory and deletes it in a finally block, which is WHY write_scope is temp_dir and why escalation_class is owner_word rather than none.

proves: THAT A SECOND INSTRUMENT CAN DISAGREE WITH THE FIRST AND BE RIGHT, measured on this repository's own artefact. native.pe.authenticode reads dwLength=48 / wRevision=0x200 / revision_is_2_0=true off the fixture and is not wrong; OpenSSL rejects the same 40 bytes with ASN1_get_object:too long and is not wrong either. The fixture's certificate is the ASCII string ARSENAL-FIXTURE-NOT-A-REAL-SIGNATURE.

THAT Q6.crypto HAS A SECOND FAMILY. Q6 measured 1 of 2 working, one instrument, one family, which is the state the independence gate exists to refuse. This entry carries certificate-verifier, a genuinely different question from reading the table.
does_not_prove:
THAT THESE TWO INSTRUMENTS ARE FULLY INDEPENDENT, AND THE MISSION'S OWN OUTPUT SAYS SO. Verified in a Q6 mission on 2026-10-02: independence PASSES with '2 capabilities across 2 instruments (openssl+pefile, pefile) carrying 2 distinct families'. Read that instrument list rather than the verdict: the two SHARE pefile. This entry uses pefile only to LOCATE the SECURITY directory; the DECISION is OpenSSL's DER decoder, which is a genuinely separate implementation and is where the disagreement with native.pe.authenticode actually comes from.

The shared part is not decorative. If pefile misread the DATA_DIRECTORY entry, both instruments would be wrong together and the second opinion would be worthless -- the independence gate counts instruments, and two instruments that share a locator are only as independent as that locator. It is recorded here rather than left to be discovered later, because a partial overlap that is written down is a limitation and the same overlap written down as '2 independent instruments' is a false claim.

THAT ANYTHING IS TRUSTED, SIGNED OR SAFE. ASN.1 PARSING IS NOT TRUST. der_parsed:true means the bytes are well-formed ASN.1 -- nothing here checks that the chain roots anywhere, that the digest matches the file, or that the signer is who it claims.

THAT A REAL SIGNATURE WAS REJECTED. What was rejected is a fixture whose payload SAYS it is not one. Rejecting it proves the instrument can tell DER from non-DER; it says nothing about a genuine signature, because this repository has no genuine signed binary to point it at.
ANYTHING ABOUT TRUST BOUNDARIES. Not a Q5 instrument and not offered as one.

THAT pefile IS WRONG. It is not. It reads a header and reports it accurately; this tool checks the layer below. Two instruments each being right is the whole mechanism, and collapsing either into 'the other one is broken' destroys it.

CORRECTED TWICE, both times by running it rather than reading it. capabilities.title: Parse a pcap with no library and no tshark: counts packets, flows, ports and DNS direction
capabilities.scope_note: READS ONE FILE. No network, no execution, no writes, no temp files. It parses the 24-byte global header, the 16-byte per-packet headers, and then Ethernet / VLAN / IPv4 / IPv6 / TCP / UDP far enough to count.
capabilities.composition_note:
ADDED FOR INDEPENDENCE, AND THE INDEPENDENCE IS REAL THIS TIME. net.pcap.analyse answers capture questions by shelling out to TShark 4.6.8, and it was the arsenal's ONLY capture-analysis instrument, so Q4.data measured one instrument in one family and the independence gate could never pass there. A second front-end over the same C library would have been one implementation held twice; this is a from-scratch reader in pure Python with no third-party dependency at all, so agreement between the two is corroboration rather than a restatement.

MEASURED 2026-10-02, all five lab captures, both instruments, packets AND DNS direction:
  dns-basic.pcap 4/4 dns 2/2 vs 2/2 | dns-txt.pcap 4/4 dns 2/2 vs 2/2 |
  http-basic.pcap 10/10 dns 0/0 vs 0/0 | odd-port.pcap 26/26 dns 0/0 vs 0/0 |
  tls-clienthello.pcap 14/14 dns 0/0 vs 0/0 -- ALL AGREE.

AND THE FIRST COMPARISON ATTEMPT WAS WRONG, WHICH IS WORTH RECORDING. It reported a disagreement: tshark '0/0' against the reader's 2/2. The cause was the comparison script, not either instrument -- tshark's dns.flags.response prints the STRINGS 'False' and 'True', and the script compared them to '0' and '1', so it counted nothing and reported a phantom discrepancy. tshark in fact sees all four DNS rows and agrees exactly.

That is the 'an error is not a zero' trap in a new costume, and it nearly became a recorded finding about a working tool. A disagreement between instruments is the most interesting thing this pair could produce, which is precisely why a buggy comparator is dangerous here: it manufactures the interesting result.

inputs.name: capture
inputs.note: a classic libpcap file. The corpus is GENERATED, not committed: net-reverse/lab/gen-pcaps.mjs writes five synthetic captures to %TEMP%\net-reverse-lab\pcaps (override NET_REVERSE_PCAP_DIR).

facts.note: dns_queries and dns_responses counted from bit 15 of the DNS flags word. Measured: 2 queries and 2 responses on each of dns-basic and dns-txt, 0 and 0 on the other three. A COUNT TAKEN FROM A HEURISTIC, not from dissection: this reader matches on port 53 and reads two bytes. TShark dissects and agrees here, which is what makes the number worth having -- on a capture with a non-standard port or a malformed DNS header, only the dissector would be right. RE-TYPED and RENAMED 2026-10-03. The old name said direction and the old type said verdict; the emitted value is an INTEGER COUNT: measured live, dns_queries = 2 and dns_responses = 2 on dns-basic.pcap, and pcap_reader.py counts them flat (dns_queries at :68, :123, :144, :166). A verdict is one of confirmed/likely/speculative/unresolved/refused and an integer count is none of those, so the fact was claiming an evidence class it could never carry. The packet counts this entry used to publish as `pcap.counts` are DELETED rather than retyped: fact_map bound them to a stdout key `counts` that pcap_reader.py never emits -- measured by running it, the emitted keys are bytes_on_wire, captured_bytes, distinct_flows, dns_queries, dns_responses, exit, file, frames_over_snaplen, ipv4, ipv6, limits, ok, other_proto, packets, pcap, tcp, top_ports, udp -- so the fact was unreachable, and a fact nobody can produce is worse than no fact. The flat counter list is preserved here as what the emitter actually gives.

requires.install_note: NO THIRD-PARTY DEPENDENCY. struct and ipaddress are in the standard library, which is the whole point: scapy and dpkt are not installed on this station, and a second reader built on either would have had to be installed first. Runs in well under a second, which makes it the cheapest cross-check in the arsenal.

reach.proc_spawn_note:
CORRECTED BY R8, WHICH WAS RIGHT AND I WAS WRONG. This first read proc_spawn:false on the reasoning that nothing is shelled out to. That reasoning conflated two things: running `python pcap_reader.py` IS a child process, and R8's floor says exactly that -- any capability with a probe.command or an invoke.runner spawns something, precisely so that deleting the declaration makes it falsifiable.

What actually distinguishes this entry is narrower and is the claim worth making: it spawns ONLY its own interpreter and no analysis tool. net.pcap.analyse spawns TShark; this spawns python and reads the bytes itself. That is why the two are independent rather than one implementation behind two front-ends.

proves: THAT Q4.data HAS A SECOND, GENUINELY INDEPENDENT IMPLEMENTATION. Measured on all five lab captures: packet counts agree with TShark 4.6.8 (4/4, 4/4, 10/10, 26/26, 14/14) and DNS query/response counts agree too (2/2, 2/2, and 0/0 on the three with no DNS). Two implementations written against the same file format in two languages is what corroboration means.
THAT A CAPTURE CAN BE READ WITHOUT ANY ANALYSIS TOOL. No tshark, no scapy, no dpkt, no subprocess. If TShark disappeared this capability would still answer.
does_not_prove: ANYTHING ABOUT CONTENT. There is no reassembly and no TLS decode. A DNS name split across packets is not read, and an encrypted payload is not decoded. Agreement with TShark is corroboration of the COUNTS only, and neither instrument here says anything about what any packet contained.

THAT pcap.dns_direction IS A DISSECTION. It is a port-53 match plus one bit. On a capture using a non-standard DNS port, or carrying a malformed DNS header, this reader would be wrong and TShark would be right. The two agree on THIS corpus, which is a fact about the corpus and not a general property.

THAT THE CORPUS IS REPRESENTATIVE. All five captures are SYNTHETIC and generated by net-reverse/lab/gen-pcaps.mjs. Two readers agreeing on five generated files is evidence about the format and about those files; it is not evidence about real traffic.

THAT THE FIRST COMPARISON SHOWED A DISAGREEMENT. It did not. That was a bug in the comparison script and is recorded in composition_note so the phantom discrepancy is not rediscovered and mistaken for a finding.

probe.run_summary_note: RE-MEASURED 2026-10-04 against seven purpose-built fixtures, old parser vs new, same bytes. Three measured defects are fixed and the fix is proved by before/after, not by assertion: (1) IPv4 fragment continuation -- the old parser ignored frag_off and read a continuation fragment's PAYLOAD as a transport header, reporting ports 21317 and 17231, which are ASCII 'SECO' (0x53 0x45 / 0x43 0x4F) and nothing else; now fragments_first / fragments_continuation are counted and reported and no port is invented. (2) VLAN TPID -- only 0x8100 was unwrapped, so 802.1ad QinQ (0x88a8) and legacy QinQ (0x9100) parsed as all-zero with exit 0, while the code's own comment claimed 'any number of stacked VLAN tags'. (3) IPv6 -- l4 was hardcoded at l3+40, so Hop-by-Hop and Routing extension headers shifted the transport header and the reader reported tcp=0 / other_proto=1 / no ports for frames plainly carrying TCP at 443. Two control captures are byte-identical old and new, so the fix does not regress the happy path. What remains declared and unfixed: no reassembly, no TLS, no fragment reassembly, and DNS is still a port-53 plus flag-bit heuristic.

capabilities.title: Read a PE's mitigation posture with rabin2: stack canary, injection protection, retguard, checksum, image base
capabilities.scope_note: READS ONE FILE via rabin2 -I. No network, no execution of the target, no writes, no temp files. rabin2 is spawned as a child process.
capabilities.composition_note:
REGISTERED BECAUSE AN AUDIT FOUND IT INSTALLED, PAID FOR, AND UNWIRED. radare2 6.2.2 is pinned in manifests/tools.json, smoke-tested in scripts/smoke-tools.ps1, and present on disk at Static-Reversing/radare2/ -- and a grep for radare2, rabin2 and rizin across the whole registry returned ZERO capability hits. This is the same discovery as capa (installed, working, no entry), found a second time by auditing INVENTORY rather than intentions.

IT IS ALSO THE ONLY INSTRUMENT HERE THAT ANSWERS A QUESTION NOTHING ELSE ASKS. native.pe.container reads ASLR; native.pe.authenticode reads the certificate table. Neither reports whether a binary carries a stack canary, whether the image is marked as vulnerable to control-flow hijack, or whether a checksum is present. Mitigation posture is what a reviewer asks before deciding whether a crash is interesting, and it was absent from a 26-capability arsenal.

IT IS A FOURTH INSTRUMENT AND A GENUINELY DIFFERENT IMPLEMENTATION: pefile reads the IMAGE structure in Python, rabin2 is a C tool with its own format layer. The independence gate counts families, so a fourth reading from a different codebase is worth more here than another pefile wrapper would be.

inputs.name: binary
inputs.note: a Windows PE. Measured: crackme-corpus/out/c01-stringobf.exe.

facts.note: arch, bits, class, bintype, baddr, binsz, endian, machine, os, subsys, compiler, lang. Measured: x86 / 64 / PE32+ / pe / baddr 0x140000000 / binsz 143872.

canary, injprot, retguard, nx, pic, relocs, stripped, crypto. Measured on c01-stringobf.exe: canary true, nx true, pic true, injprot false, retguard false, crypto false, relocs false, stripped false. PRESENCE FLAGS FROM ONE IMPLEMENTATION.

tools.name: rabin2
tools.note: expect was the phrase 'info block with arch and bintype', which is a DESCRIPTION and cannot occur in output. Replaced with a literal the output actually contains, measured 'bintype  pe'.

requires.install_note: ALREADY INSTALLED. Nothing to download, nothing to build, no PATH change. Portable build pinned at 6.2.2; a 6.2.0 build also exists on disk and the wrapper deliberately points at the pinned one.

reach.proc_spawn_note: rabin2 is spawned as a child. The target is read, never executed.

proves: THAT THE ARSENAL CAN NOW ANSWER 'what hardening does this binary carry', WHICH IT COULD NOT BEFORE. Measured on c01-stringobf.exe in 0.4 s: canary true, nx true, pic true, injprot false, retguard false, crypto false. No other capability reports any of these.

THAT A FOURTH INDEPENDENT NATIVE INSTRUMENT EXISTS AND IS NOT pefile WEARING A HAT. rabin2 is a C tool with its own PE format layer; native.pe.container and native.pe.authenticode are pefile. Verified by grep: before this entry, radare2/rabin2/rizin appeared in ZERO capabilities.
does_not_prove: THAT THE BINARY IS HARDENED. These are presence flags from ONE implementation, not a hardening assessment. `canary true` means a stack-protection cookie symbol was found; it does not mean the buffer it protects is bounded, and it says nothing about whether the cookie is checked correctly.

THAT ANY MITIGATION IS CORRECTLY APPLIED. A present-but-ineffective mitigation reads exactly like an effective one here. `nx true` is rabin2 reporting the NX-compatible bit, and a PE can carry that bit and still be marked executable -- which is why the field is reported but not asserted.

THAT `crypto true` MEANS TRUSTED. It means a signature directory is PRESENT, which is a trigger to ask native.pe.authenticode or native.signature.certverify. That the arsenal's own signed fixture is not a real signature is already measured.
THAT AN ABSENT FLAG MEANS ABSENT HARDENING. As with every instrument here, a field rabin2 does not report is unknown, not false.
